questions.prompt: What does Anthropic's evaluator-optimizer pattern do?

options.text: One call makes a response and another evaluates it and gives feedback, in a loop
options.explanation: Right. This is Anthropic's own description of the pattern.

options.text: It splits a job into parts and runs every part at the same moment on different models
options.explanation: That is parallelization, a different pattern in the same post.

options.text: It sends every output to a person, who writes the next prompt for the model by hand
options.explanation: The pattern uses a second model as the evaluator, not a person for each round.

questions.prompt: Which rubric line fits the style Claude's outcomes page asks for?

options.text: The video looks good to most viewers and feels right for the brand overall
options.explanation: Looks good is vague. The page says vague criteria produce noisy evaluations.

options.text: A checkable line, such as "the logo is readable in the final two seconds"
options.explanation: Right. The page prefers explicit, gradeable criteria. The ad line is our example in the same style.

options.text: The agent says it is confident that the work is done, with no further checks
options.explanation: The agent's confidence is not a check on the work. The grader scores the work against the rubric.

questions.prompt: Why does Claude's grader run in a separate context window?

options.text: So the grader is not influenced by the implementation choices of the main agent
options.explanation: Right. This is the reason the outcomes page gives.

options.text: So the grader can use a bigger model than the main agent does, at a lower price
options.explanation: The page gives a different reason: keeping the grader free of the main agent's choices.

options.text: So the main agent never learns what the grader said, and tries a fresh idea each time
options.explanation: The grader's explanation is handed back to the agent for the next iteration.
